short: A piece of text in code, written inside quote marks, like "Hello".
everyday: The exact wording of a templated message. It goes out word for word.

short: A note in code that starts with #. Python ignores it.
everyday: Internal case notes: useful for the team, invisible to the customer.

short: A name with a value attached, like balance = 455. The value can change.
everyday: A labelled field on the customer screen: the label stays, the value inside changes.

short: Text with an f before the quote, where {curly brackets} are filled in with values: f"Hi {name}".
everyday: A templated message with the customer's details merged in.

short: Storing money as a whole number of the smallest unit (pence) instead of decimals, so there are no rounding errors.
everyday: Why a statement should never be 1p out.

short: Code that repeats: a for loop runs once for each item in a list; a while loop runs as long as something is true.
everyday: Working through the queue: the same steps for every case.

short: A named, reusable set of steps that takes inputs and returns an answer. Defined with def.
everyday: A saved macro or canned response: write once, use all day.

short: A named input to a function, like amount in def card_fee(amount). The value you pass in when calling is the argument.
everyday: The blanks in a template that get filled in each time.

short: An ordered collection of values in square brackets: [12.50, 3.20, 45.00]. Positions start at 0.
everyday: The lines on a statement, in order.

short: A collection of key-value pairs in curly brackets: {"name": "Amira", "card_status": "active"}.
everyday: One customer record: field labels and their values.

short: Python's error report. Read it from the bottom: the error type, then the line where it happened.
everyday: A decline reason code, plus exactly where in the process it failed.

short: An unusual but possible input, like an empty list, zero, or a negative amount, that code must handle correctly.
everyday: The awkward cases that aren't in the script: the customer with no transactions, or the refund bigger than the payment.

short: Software that stores data in an organised way and answers questions about it quickly.
everyday: Everything behind the CRM search box.

short: A set of records of one kind in a database, made of rows (records) and columns (fields).
everyday: One spreadsheet: customers, cards or transactions.

short: Structured Query Language: the language for asking a database questions, e.g. SELECT name FROM customers.
everyday: Looking up thousands of accounts at once instead of one by one.

short: A column whose value uniquely identifies each row, usually id.
everyday: A customer number: no two customers share one.

short: A column that holds another table's primary key, linking the two, like cards.customer_id.
everyday: "Customer ref: 1" written on a case, pointing at the customer record.

short: A version control tool that records snapshots of your project, so you can see history and go back.
everyday: A full case history for your code.

short: A project folder tracked by Git, including its full history.
everyday: The case file.

short: A saved snapshot of your changes in Git, with a message explaining what changed.
everyday: A case note: what you did and why.

short: A website that hosts Git repositories online, for backup, sharing, code review and your portfolio.
everyday: The shared case system, compared with a private notebook.

short: A separate line of work in Git, so you can change things without touching main until they're reviewed.
everyday: A draft reply you can edit freely before it's sent.

short: A request on GitHub to review and merge your branch's changes into main.
everyday: A refund over your limit that needs a second approver.

short: Application Programming Interface: a defined way for software to send requests to another system and get responses.
everyday: The front desk: apps ask in a standard way and get an answer, without ever going into the back office.

short: A message sent to an API, made up of a method (GET, POST…), a path, headers and sometimes a body.
everyday: A customer's question, plus their ID and any forms they've filled in.

short: What an API sends back: a status code, headers and usually a JSON body.
everyday: The answer the front desk gives, with an outcome code.

short: A three-digit number in every response: 2xx worked, 4xx the caller's request was wrong, 5xx the server broke.
everyday: Decline codes for the web.

short: A text format for data, with objects in {} and lists in []. It's how most APIs send data.
everyday: A standard form layout every system can read.

short: Code that checks other code gives the right answers, run automatically, e.g. assert card_fee(100) == 1.50.
everyday: A mystery shopper you brief once, who checks the process every time anything changes.

short: The most popular Python testing tool. It finds functions named test_… and runs them.
everyday: The QA team that runs every check and reports what failed.

short: A tool that packages an app with everything it needs into an image that runs the same anywhere.
everyday: Shipping a card terminal already set up, instead of posting setup instructions.

short: The sealed bundle Docker builds from a Dockerfile: code, libraries and settings together.
everyday: A sealed, labelled meal kit.

short: A running copy of a Docker image.
everyday: The meal kit, cooked and on the table.

short: Automatically checking (and often deploying) code on every change, with lint, tests and so on. A failing step blocks the rest.
everyday: A four-eyes approval check that never takes a day off.

short: The merchant's bank or payment provider, which accepts card payments on the merchant's behalf.
everyday: The café's side of the payment.

short: The cardholder's bank, which issued the card and approves or declines payments.
everyday: Probably the company you work for now.

short: The network, such as Visa or Mastercard, that routes payments between acquirers and issuers and sets the rules.
everyday: The motorway system and highway code that every payment travels by.

short: The real-time approve-or-decline step of a card payment. Funds are held, but not yet moved.
everyday: Why a payment shows as pending.

short: Confirming the final details of authorised transactions, usually in batches later the same day.
everyday: When pending becomes posted.

short: When money actually moves from issuer to acquirer to merchant, minus fees, often one or two working days later.
everyday: The day the café actually gets paid.

short: A disputed card payment reversed through the card scheme's rules, initiated by the cardholder's issuer.
everyday: The dispute process you know, seen from the systems' side.

short: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard: the security rules for anyone storing, processing or transmitting card data.
everyday: Never asking for the full PIN or security code, written into how systems are built.

short: Replacing a real card number with a random stand-in (a token) that's useless if stolen.
everyday: A cloakroom ticket: worthless on its own, but it gets the right coat back at the desk.

short: A PSD2 rule: payers prove who they are with two of three factors: something they know, have or are.
everyday: Why customers have to approve online payments in their banking app.

short: An action is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.
everyday: A customer taps Pay twice but is only charged once.

short: A unique ID sent with a request (usually in an Idempotency-Key header) so the server can spot retries and return the saved result instead of repeating the action.
everyday: A refund reference number: submit it twice and the system says "already done".

short: A set of states plus the allowed moves between them. Code refuses any move that isn't allowed.
everyday: A case workflow where Resolve is greyed out until the case has been reviewed.

short: A record of every money movement as entries that sum to zero. Balances are worked out from it, never stored separately.
everyday: The transaction history that always explains the balance, line by line.

short: The part of an app users don't see: servers, APIs and databases. The frontend is the screens they do see.
everyday: The back office, compared with the shop floor.

short: A text window where you type commands like git commit or docker build.
everyday: Typing instructions directly instead of clicking buttons.
